arxiv.org: arXiv:2610.26664v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents deployed inside organizations can pose an insider threat if they make mistakes, are compromised by an attacker, or pursue misaligned objectives. We propose honeypots as an AI control method to improve the security of internal agent deployments. Rather than only using honeypots for pre-deployment evaluations, defenders should plant decoy opportunities for harmful actions throughout the production environment to detect misbehavior, incriminate malicious agents, and deter attacks. Such honeypots can elicit misbehavior under real deployment conditions, identify malicious agents even if chain-of-thought monitorability degrades, provide reliable warnings about agent misbehavior to security teams, and scale cheaply to many agent instances. The presence of honeypots also introduces uncertainty about which opportunities are real, thus deterring malicious agents from attacking and reducing the rate of misbehavior. We discuss the limitations of honeypots and give reasons to expect them to remain effective as agent capabilities increase. Finally, we outline key research questions to measure and improve the effectiveness of honeypots: testing the robustness of honeypots, comparing their detection effectiveness with other monitoring methods, understanding their incrimination and deterrence effects, and building supporting infrastructure.

body: technologyreview.com: _____________ THE PLACE Pyeongtaek, South Korea Generative AI models run on powerful chips known as GPUs, which depend on stacks of specialized memory chips packaged with the processor. To meet growing demand for memory, Samsung is building a massive new semiconductor manufacturing complex in Pyeongtaek, South Korea. Three fabs already operate around the clock, and a fourth is coming online. Construction of a fifth was halted during a drop in demand for memory chips in 2024 but restarted when the AI boom sent demand soaring. It’s just before noon on a Monday, and construction workers are pouring out of Samsung’s fabs in Pyeongtaek, a farming city south of Seoul where rice paddies abut a sprawling chipmaking complex. Thousands of workers, dressed head to toe in black with sky-blue vests, take off helmets bearing their names and fab numbers. They walk to lunch, sweaty and flushed, in chunky sneakers capped with yellow rubber toe guards. Some hop on scooters or motorcycles to get around the campus, which covers an area about the size of New York City’s Central Park. They’ll dine at buffets, diners, and beef stew joints, walking past banners advertising short-term leases for studio apartments. Some stop by real estate offices to inquire, stepping up to the same counters where Samsung’s salaried engineers buy new homes . In front of the fourth fab, I meet Choi Hye-rin, a 35-year-old safety officer, as she wipes her forehead with a handkerchief. At dawn, she boarded one of the shuttle buses that ferry workers in from Songtan, an older, scrappier district. She oversees the safety of a crew responsible for building cable ducts. She writes reports, inspects equipment, and checks the chemicals the workers handle. She’s one of hundreds of women working on site, many employed as spotters who walk ahead of heavy equipment. Safety is a big deal here. After lunch, construction picks right back up. Excavators move past rust-red steel structures rising high under tower cranes. Banne

arxiv.org: arXiv:2610.26287v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Modern robotic photography requires understanding photographic intent, planning camera motions, and producing aesthetically pleasing images in complex environments. We present RoboPhoto-VLA, a unified Vision-Language-Action framework that jointly models perception, reasoning, and camera control for autonomous robotic photography. RoboPhoto-VLA incorporates PhotoCoT for structured action planning and Aesthetic Direct Preference Optimization (ADPO) to align camera behaviors with human aesthetic preferences. To facilitate training and evaluation, we construct OpenPhotography, a robotic photography dataset with language-guided demonstrations. Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that RoboPhoto-VLA produces photographs better aligned with human aesthetic preferences while generalizing effectively to unseen subjects, viewpoints, poses, and complex photographic instructions.

arxiv.org: arXiv:2610.26487v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The limited onboard computing resources of robots make the inference demands of vision-language-action (VLA) models costly to accommodate. Reducing these demands through aggressive compression, however, can degrade manipulation performance beyond what supervised fine-tuning alone recovers. We present SPAR (Structural Pruning and Action Recovery), which simultaneously prunes the hidden and feed-forward intermediate dimensions of the large language model (LLM) backbone through pruning-aware tuning, then applies reinforcement learning (RL) to recover policy performance. Applied to $\pi_{0.5}$, SPAR reduces the language backbone from 2.34B to 0.09B parameters and the full model from 3.37B to 1.12B, removing approximately 96% and 67% of their parameters, respectively. At this compression level, RL raises average success across the four LIBERO suites from 84.55% to 93.45%, an 8.90-percentage-point gain. The compressed policy achieves a $1.98\times$ full-policy inference speedup over the unpruned model. These results identify substantial intermediate-dimension redundancy and show that post-pruning RL can recover manipulation performance in compact policies.

body: technologyreview.com: Imagine your company just discovered electricity. At first only a few machines run on it, and nobody worries about efficiency — consumption is low and the value is obvious. But once electricity becomes infrastructure, every process depends on it, and the question changes from can we use it? to how efficiently are we using it? Enterprise AI is going through the same shift. What began as isolated chatbot and copilot experiments is becoming a foundational layer of the business, with models, agents, and data increasingly interconnected in production workloads. The important question stops being what a token or GPU-hour costs. It becomes how efficiently the AI environment converts paid capacity into useful business outcomes. That s the metric worth tracking: effective cost per useful outcome — the total platform, model, operations, and capacity cost required to complete work the business can actually use, whether a resolved request or a completed workflow. Three ways to run AI Utilization is central to the economics. Directing more work to paid-for capacity lowers effective unit cost; idle GPUs, fragmented workloads, and oversized models all raise the cost of every useful result. Enterprises generally choose among three models: A bespoke stack — procuring infrastructure and controls in-house. This approach is flexible, but it creates a continuing burden, since teams must revalidate the environment as models and policies change. On-demand consumption — hyperscalers reduce the assembly burden and suit low or uncertain demand, but charges rise with every prompt or agent action. An integrated private AI platform — owned or dedicated capacity paired with a validated stack. The advantage isn t free inference; it s control over efficiency levers like scheduling, model selection, GPU partitioning, and cache management. The right model depends on the workload. b: technologyreview.com: AI adoption by industry shows what other sectors can learn
body: technologyreview.com: The current narrative around artificial intelligence in the workplace is largely driven by Silicon Valley. But treating the tech sector as an island misses the actual trends in technology adoption–tech is just the first industry in line. As generative AI and automation tools mature, the shifts currently reshaping software engineering and product management will inevitably filter into healthcare, education, retail, and manufacturing. The variation in adoption rates today isn t a sign that non-tech industries are falling behind, but rather a reflection of the different speeds at which industries absorb new workflows. For leaders and their teams outside of tech, this differential pace provides a practical blueprint for how AI adoption unfolds, and where the opportunities lie. The AI adoption spectrum by industry Recent survey data from TripleTen highlights just how stark the current adoption curve is across different sectors of the economy (see Figure 1). Figure 1: The AI adoption curve remains steep across industries, but non-tech industry adoption rates are increasing. Source : TripleTen , 2026 While tech leads the way, finance emerges as a clear second: 48% of finance workers have been asked to use AI chatbots, and 32% have been asked to automate parts of their workflow. This demonstrates how rapidly knowledge work integrates AI once clear use cases emerge. By contrast, sectors like healthcare (18% asked to use chatbots) and education (25%) reflect lower initial exposure. Because these broad industry categories encompass a mix of specialized hands-on professionals, clinical or instructional personnel, and back-office administrative staff, universal adoption was never going to happen overnight. Integrating automated tools into compliance-heavy or human-facing operations requires a more deliberate pace, which is reflected by the lower numbers. arxiv.org: arXiv:2610.24454v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-agent scientific discovery with large language models raises a coupled learning problem: research assignments determine both which experiments are pursued and the experiences from which agents adapt. We introduce MELD, a unified hierarchical test-time training framework that jointly adapts a team-level Coordinator policy and agent-level individual Scientist policies within a single discovery process. The Coordinator generates a joint portfolio of search branches and research directives over a shared derivation tree, while Scientists develop hypotheses and execution plans implemented by a shared frozen Executor. Both levels receive alternating GRPO-style parameter updates under a shared smooth best-of-budget objective, allowing team organization and individual research behavior to co-evolve in a recursive self-improvement loop. Our analysis establishes objective alignment for the hierarchy, characterizes conditions for coordination gains over independent parallel discovery and the first-order benefit of private adaptation, and derives a finite-budget regret bound for adapted models. On 22 MLGym and MLE-bench tasks, MELD is best on 20 of them and achieves the highest aggregate normalized scores on MLGym, using a 4B backbone for coordination and research. Most baselines use proprietary Scientists, and all systems share one frozen Executor.

arxiv.org: arXiv:2610.25697v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models have recently been used to discover heuristics through iterative program search, offering a promising approach to automated algorithm design. However, candidates selected by average performance may degrade across instance families, random seeds, and problem scales because mean-based objectives can obscure rare but severe failures. We propose CVaR-RMD, a risk-sensitive evolutionary framework that uses an LLM to mutate executable heuristic programs and ranks candidates by empirical conditional value-at-risk over heterogeneous evaluation conditions. Across three combinatorial optimization domains, CVaR-based selection improves upper-tail performance and reduces failure rates while maintaining competitive mean performance. These gains persist on larger unseen instances and independently curated within-domain benchmarks

arxiv.org: arXiv:2610.25867v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An evidence-review system must allocate additional model judgments and control their use. We study these software decisions on 6,164 frozen manufacturing source-task pairs. Benefit-targeted routing learns recovered agreement minus newly introduced disagreement. On the original 300-case test, 60 consultations yield 202/231 agreements with two human references versus 189/218 for a logistic-risk router. An additional 300 cases were independently annotated twice using equal frozen evidence. Without retraining the historical policies, the corresponding counts are 164/190 versus 163/193; the differences do not resolve an advantage. Strict scalar-Ridge controls share preprocessing, regularization and fitting, and remain inconclusive. Quotation and requested-state replacement gates retain rejected cases and budget costs; their joint gate rejects one original and two additional consultations without changing primary outcomes. Evidence ablations, fusion and bounded updates supply further controls. A completed 200-pair identity audit yields 97.45 percent weighted merge precision after eight author adjudications. This audits a provisional map, while prospective company-disjoint performance remains untested.
